blocks.body:
On the page on [[metric-spaces]], continuity of a map between metric spaces turns out to have a description that never mentions distance: $f$ is continuous exactly when the preimage of every open set is open. Many different metrics, such as the taxicab, Euclidean and maximum metrics on $\mathbb{R}^2$, have the same open sets and therefore the same continuous maps. For continuity, only the open sets matter.

Topology takes this seriously: a topological space is a set together with a choice of which subsets count as open, subject to three simple rules. This lets us work with spaces that have no natural metric, such as spaces built by gluing (a torus made from a square), spaces of functions, and the Zariski topology of algebraic geometry. The page ends with connectedness and the intermediate value theorem in its general form.

blocks.title: Topological space
Examples
blocks.body:
- Metric topology. In a metric space, call $U$ open if around each of its points it contains some ball $B(x, r)$. This satisfies the three axioms; the finite-intersection rule uses the minimum of finitely many radii, and fails for infinite intersections: $\bigcap_{n \ge 1} (-\tfrac1n, \tfrac1n) = \{0\}$ is not open in $\mathbb{R}$.
- Equivalent metrics. On $\mathbb{R}^2$ the maximum, Euclidean and taxicab metrics satisfy $d_\infty \le d_2 \le d_1 \le 2d_\infty$, so every ball for one contains a concentric ball for each other, and all three give the same topology.
- Discrete topology: every subset is open. Indiscrete topology: only $\varnothing$ and $X$.
- Cofinite topology on an infinite set $X$: the open sets are $\varnothing$ and the sets with finite complement. On $\mathbb{C}$, this is the Zariski topology, whose closed sets are the zero sets of polynomials in one variable.
- Finite examples. On $X = \{a, b\}$ there are exactly four topologies: indiscrete, discrete, $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, X\}$ and $\{\varnothing, \{b\}, X\}$. A three-point set has $29$.
- Subspace topology. If $A \subseteq X$, the open sets of $A$ are the sets $U \cap A$ with $U$ open in $X$. For instance $[0, \tfrac12)$ is open in the subspace $[0,1]$ of $\mathbb{R}$, though not open in $\mathbb{R}$.
- Product topology on $X \times Y$: a set is open if it is a union of "open rectangles" $U \times V$. On $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$ this gives the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}^2$.

blocks.title: Closure and the Hausdorff property
blocks.body:
Let $A \subseteq X$. The closure $\overline{A}$ is the intersection of all closed sets containing $A$ (the smallest closed superset of $A$). A space is Hausdorff if any two distinct points have disjoint open neighbourhoods.

Every metric space is Hausdorff (use balls of radius half the distance). A cofinite space on an infinite set is not: two nonempty open sets each omit only finitely many points, so they intersect. Without the Hausdorff property sequences behave strangely: in $\mathbb{Z}$ with the cofinite topology, $x_n = n$ converges to every point, since an open set containing $p$ omits only finitely many integers. In general spaces sequences do not even detect closures or continuity, which is why everything here is phrased with open sets.

blocks.title: Lemma: points of the closure
blocks.body: Let $A \subseteq X$ and $x \in X$. Then $x \in \overline{A}$ if and only if every open neighbourhood of $x$ meets $A$.

Suppose some open $U 
i x$ satisfies $U \cap A = \varnothing$. Then $X \setminus U$ is a closed set containing $A$ but not $x$, so $x 
otin \overline{A}$. Conversely, if $x 
otin \overline{A}$ there is a closed $C \supseteq A$ with $x 
otin C$; then $U = X \setminus C$ is an open neighbourhood of $x$ disjoint from $A$.

blocks.title: Continuity and homeomorphism
blocks.body: A map $f\colon X \to Y$ between topological spaces is continuous if $f^{-1}(V)$ is open in $X$ for every open $V \subseteq Y$. It is a homeomorphism if it is a bijection and both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are continuous. Spaces related by a homeomorphism are topologically identical: the bijection matches their open sets exactly.

blocks.title: Characterisations of continuity

blocks.body:
(1) and (2) are equivalent because $f^{-1}(Y \setminus C) = X \setminus f^{-1}(C)$.

(1) implies (3). Let $x \in \overline{A}$ and let $V$ be an open neighbourhood of $f(x)$. Then $f^{-1}(V)$ is an open neighbourhood of $x$, so by the lemma it contains a point $a \in A$, and $f(a) \in V \cap f(A)$. Every neighbourhood of $f(x)$ meets $f(A)$, so $f(x) \in \overline{f(A)}$.

(3) implies (2). Let $C \subseteq Y$ be closed and $A = f^{-1}(C)$. Then $f(\overline{A}) \subseteq \overline{f(A)} \subseteq \overline{C} = C$, so $\overline{A} \subseteq f^{-1}(C) = A$. Hence $A = \overline{A}$ is closed.

For composites, $(g \circ f)^{-1}(W) = f^{-1}(g^{-1}(W))$ is open whenever $W$ is. The equivalence with epsilon–delta continuity for metric spaces is proved on [[metric-spaces]].

blocks.title: Example 1: checking the definitions
blocks.body:
Let $X = \{a, b, c\}$.

1. Is $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{b\}, X\}$ a topology on $X$? Is $\{\varnothing, \{a\}, \{a, b\}, X\}$?
2. Let $X_d$ and $X_i$ denote $X$ with the discrete and the indiscrete topology. Which of the identity maps $X_d \to X_i$ and $X_i \to X_d$ is continuous?
3. Show that the map $f\colon [0, 2\pi) \to S^1$, $f(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)$, is a continuous bijection but not a homeomorphism.
blocks.solution:
1. The first is not a topology: $\{a\} \cup \{b\} = \{a, b\}$ is missing. The second is: it contains $\varnothing$ and $X$, and it is a chain $\varnothing \subseteq \{a\} \subseteq \{a,b\} \subseteq X$, so unions and intersections of its members are again members.

2. $X_d \to X_i$ is continuous, because every subset of $X_d$ is open, so any preimage is open. $X_i \to X_d$ is not: $\{a\}$ is open in $X_d$, and its preimage $\{a\}$ is not open in $X_i$. More open sets in the domain, or fewer in the target, only help continuity.

3. Continuity and bijectivity are clear. The inverse is not continuous at $(1,0)$: the set $U = [0, \pi)$ is open in the subspace $[0, 2\pi)$, but $f(U)$, the upper half of the circle including $(1,0)$ and excluding $(-1, 0)$, is not open in $S^1$, since points $(\cos t, \sin t)$ with $t$ slightly less than $2\pi$ are arbitrarily close to $(1,0)$ and not in $f(U)$. So $(f^{-1})^{-1}(U) = f(U)$ is not open. By contrast $h(x) = \tan(\pi(x - \tfrac12))$ is a homeomorphism $(0,1) \to \mathbb{R}$, with continuous inverse $y \mapsto \tfrac12 + \tfrac1\pi\arctan y$; boundedness is not a topological property.

blocks.title: Connectedness
blocks.body:
A space $X$ is connected if it cannot be written as $X = U \cup V$ with $U$, $V$ open, disjoint and nonempty. Equivalently, the only subsets of $X$ that are both open and closed are $\varnothing$ and $X$. A subset is connected if it is connected in the subspace topology. $X$ is path-connected if for any $x, y \in X$ there is a continuous $\gamma\colon [0,1] \to X$ with $\gamma(0) = x$, $\gamma(1) = y$.

Connectedness is the precise form of "being in one piece".

blocks.title: Connected subsets of the real line
blocks.body: A subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is connected if and only if it is an interval (a set $I$ such that $a, b \in I$ and $a < c < b$ imply $c \in I$). In particular $[0,1]$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are connected.

If $A$ is not an interval, pick $a, b \in A$ and $c \notin A$ with $a < c < b$. Then $A \cap (-\infty, c)$ and $A \cap (c, \infty)$ are disjoint, nonempty, open in $A$, and cover $A$, so $A$ is not connected.

Now let $[0,1] = U \cup V$ with $U, V$ disjoint, nonempty and open in $[0,1]$; we derive a contradiction. Say $0 \in U$. Let $S = \{t \in [0,1] : [0, t] \subseteq U\}$, which contains $0$, and let $s = \sup S$. Note that every $t < s$ lies in $U$, since some element of $S$ exceeds $t$.

Case $s \in U$. As $U$ is open in $[0,1]$, there is $\varepsilon > 0$ with $(s - \varepsilon, s + \varepsilon) \cap [0,1] \subseteq U$. Together with $[0, s) \subseteq U$ this gives $[0, s'] \subseteq U$ for $s' = \min(s + \varepsilon/2, 1)$, so $s' \in S$. If $s < 1$ then $s' > s$, contradicting $s = \sup S$. If $s = 1$, then $[0,1] \subseteq U$ and $V$ is empty, a contradiction.

Case $s \in V$. Then $s > 0$ (as $0 \in U$), and since $V$ is open there is $\varepsilon$ with $0 < \varepsilon \le s$ and $(s - \varepsilon, s] \subseteq V$. But points of $(s - \varepsilon, s)$ are less than $s$, hence in $U$. They would lie in $U \cap V = \varnothing$, a contradiction.

So $[0,1]$ is connected. For a general interval $I$, suppose $I = U \cup V$ is a separation and pick $u \in U$, $v \in V$, say $u < v$. Then $[u,v] \subseteq I$, and $U \cap [u,v]$, $V \cap [u,v]$ would separate $[u, v]$, which is homeomorphic to $[0,1]$ by an affine map. Contradiction.

blocks.title: Continuous images of connected spaces

blocks.body:
Suppose $f(X) = U' \cup V'$ with $U'$, $V'$ disjoint, nonempty and open in $f(X)$, say $U' = U \cap f(X)$ and $V' = V \cap f(X)$ with $U, V$ open in $Y$. Then $f^{-1}(U)$ and $f^{-1}(V)$ are open in $X$, nonempty, disjoint (a point in both would map into $U' \cap V'$) and cover $X$. This contradicts connectedness of $X$.

For 1, $f(X)$ is a connected subset of $\mathbb{R}$, hence an interval, containing $\alpha$ and $\beta$, hence everything between them.

For 2, suppose $X = U \cup V$ is a separation, and pick $x \in U$, $y \in V$ and a path $\gamma$ from $x$ to $y$. Then $\gamma^{-1}(U)$ and $\gamma^{-1}(V)$ separate $[0,1]$, contradicting the previous theorem.

blocks.title: Connected but not path-connected, and invariants
blocks.body:
The converse of part 2 fails. The topologist's sine curve
$$S = \{(x, \sin(1/x)) : 0 < x \le 1\} \cup (\{0\} \times [-1, 1])$$
is connected but not path-connected. Proof sketch: the graph part is path-connected, hence connected, and $S$ is its closure; the closure of a connected set is connected (a separation of the closure would restrict to a separation of the set). But no path joins $(0,0)$ to a point of the graph: approaching the segment, the path would have to follow the graph through infinitely many oscillations between heights $-1$ and $1$, contradicting continuity of its $y$-coordinate at the first time it reaches the segment.

Connectedness, the Hausdorff property and the number of components are preserved by homeomorphisms; such invariants are how one proves two spaces are not homeomorphic (Example 3). The [[fundamental-group|fundamental group]] and [[homology]] are far-reaching refinements.

blocks.title: Example 2: the intermediate value theorem at work
blocks.body: Prove that at every moment there are two antipodal points on the equator with exactly the same temperature (assuming temperature varies continuously).
blocks.solution:
Let $T(\theta)$ be the temperature at longitude $\theta$, a continuous $2\pi$-periodic function, and put $g(\theta) = T(\theta) - T(\theta + \pi)$. Then
$$g(\theta + \pi) = T(\theta + \pi) - T(\theta + 2\pi) = -g(\theta).$$
So $g(0)$ and $g(\pi) = -g(0)$ are zero or of opposite signs, and the intermediate value theorem on $[0, \pi]$ gives $\theta_0$ with $g(\theta_0) = 0$: the points at $\theta_0$ and $\theta_0 + \pi$ have the same temperature.

blocks.title: Example 3: the line is not the plane
blocks.body: Prove that $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{R}^2$ are not homeomorphic, and more strongly that there is no continuous injective map $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$.
blocks.solution:
Removing a point disconnects the line: $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{c\} = (-\infty, c) \cup (c, \infty)$ is a separation. Removing a point $p$ from the plane does not: any two points of $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{p\}$ can be joined by a path consisting of at most two line segments that avoids $p$ (if the segment between them passes through $p$, go instead via any point $z$ off the line through them; the two segments meet that line only at their endpoints), so $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{p\}$ is path-connected and hence connected.

Now suppose $f\colon \mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}$ is continuous and injective. Its image $I$ is connected, hence an interval, with more than one point. An interval has at most two endpoints, so we can choose $p$ with $c = f(p)$ not an endpoint of $I$. By injectivity the connected set $\mathbb{R}^2 \setminus \{p\}$ maps onto $I \setminus \{c\}$, which is not an interval and hence disconnected. Contradiction. A homeomorphism would be such a map, so $\mathbb{R} \not\cong \mathbb{R}^2$.

blocks.body:
- "Not open" does not mean "closed". In $\mathbb{R}$, $[0,1)$ is neither; $\varnothing$ and $\mathbb{R}$ are both. A space is connected precisely when $\varnothing$ and $X$ are the only sets that are both.
- Openness is relative ($[0, \tfrac12)$ is open in $[0,1]$, not in $\mathbb{R}$), and a continuous bijection need not be a homeomorphism (Example 1).
- Continuous maps need not send open sets to open sets: $x \mapsto x^2$ sends $(-1,1)$ to $[0,1)$. Continuity is about preimages.
- Connected does not imply path-connected (topologist's sine curve), though for open subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$ the two notions agree.

The next basic notion is [[compactness]]: continuous images of compact spaces are compact, and together with connectedness this gives the extreme value theorem. Quotient topologies build new spaces by gluing, leading to [[classification-of-surfaces|the classification of surfaces]], and the [[fundamental-group|fundamental group]] detects holes that connectedness cannot see. Spaces that look locally like $\mathbb{R}^n$ with smooth transition maps are [[smooth-manifolds]]. Topological spaces and continuous maps form the category $\mathbf{Top}$, a basic example on [[categories-functors]]. Infinite-dimensional [[normed-spaces|normed spaces]] carry weak topologies given by no metric.

1. Show that in the cofinite topology on an infinite set every one-point set is closed, yet the space is not Hausdorff.
2. Show that $\mathbb{Q}$, as a subspace of $\mathbb{R}$, is totally disconnected: its only nonempty connected subsets are single points.
3. Show that the circle $S^1$ is not homeomorphic to any interval of $\mathbb{R}$. (Remove a point.)
4. Prove that $f\colon X \to Y$ is continuous if and only if for every $x \in X$ and every open $V \ni f(x)$ there is an open $U \ni x$ with $f(U) \subseteq V$.
